dedupe_keys.name: princess juliana international airport reconstruction after hurricane irma sint maarten

description: This World Bank case study describes how Princess Juliana International Airport on Sint Maarten was restored after Hurricane Irma struck the island in 2017 with Category 5 intensity. Winds tore away sections of the terminal roof and doors, and saltwater flooded the interior; the one-runway airport handles nearly two million passengers a year and underpins tourism, about 45 percent of GDP and 73 percent of foreign exchange earnings, so the island was effectively cut off. Commercial flights resumed within weeks from tents and temporary pavilions, and capacity climbed from 30 to 60 percent before reconstruction began. With 105 million dollars of pre-hurricane bond debt and limited insurance proceeds, recovery relied on blended finance from the European Investment Bank and the World Bank-managed Sint Maarten Reconstruction Trust Fund, a project management unit working with Royal Schiphol Group, and phased reopening despite the pandemic, supply chain shocks and an earthquake affecting the contractor's workforce. Rebuilding added Category 5 wind-resistant entrance doors, reinforced roof anchoring and more efficient systems. Coverage: one airport, 2017 to the reopening seven years later. Access: free web feature. Licence and cost: free to read, World Bank terms. Caveats: narrative by a funder, with few engineering or cost details. It informs recovery and retrofit planning for island airports and relates to the post-hurricane supply chain study of Harvey, Irma and Maria in the catalogue.
